cycles.name: Groundwork
focuses: Learn the six main movement patterns and log a real working weight on every lift.
Build from one or two gym days a week up to three, without costing you tennis.
Film the goblet squat and Romanian deadlift every week so I can clear your technique.

paragraphs: You've been playing tennis three or four days a week but only getting to the gym once or twice. This cycle fixes that. Four weeks, three sessions, and the job is simple: learn the six main movements properly and find out what you can actually lift.

I'm not giving you a barbell yet. A movement you own at a light weight beats one you fight at a heavy one, and right now nobody has watched you squat. The goblet squat and the Romanian deadlift are the two that matter most in here. Get those right and everything after them gets easier.

By the end of four weeks you'll know your working weight on every lift, you'll be training three times a week without it wrecking your tennis, and your food will be doing some work for you instead of against you.
outcomes: Every lift calibrated to a real working weight
Squat and hinge filmed and cleared every week
Protein at every meal, 5 days a week
Body weight logged twice a week, trending down

cycles.name: Strength Engine
focuses: Drive real strength now that every lift has a calibrated load behind it.
Grow unilateral and lateral capacity, and hold the body composition trend.

paragraphs: Four weeks from now you'll know what every lift feels like, and I'll know what you can handle. That's when this changes gear.
Cycle two is where we stop teaching and start loading. Heavier, denser, and the kind of strength your tennis actually feels underneath you. But you only get there by earning it here.
Learn it now. Load it next.

cycles.name: Steel Brakes
focuses: Build eccentric strength, landing mechanics and change-of-direction tolerance.
Keep strength climbing while the tennis load stays heavy.

paragraphs: Tennis is a sport of stopping, not running. Every ball you chase ends with you putting the brakes on, and right now your body does that with nothing behind it.
Cycle three builds the brakes. It's also the gate you have to clear before we let you jump.

cycles.name: Live Wire
focuses: Turn the base into speed and power with throws, jumps and change of direction.
Sharpen first-step and recovery-step quality while holding the strength built.

paragraphs: By here you've earned the thing everybody wants to start with. Strength you can actually use inside a rally.
This is where four months of work shows up as a first step your opponent notices.

cards.title: Week One: Find Your Weights
cards.body:
The app never tells you what weight to use. You find it yourself, every set, using the RPE number on the card. RPE 7 means you finish with about three good reps left in you. RPE 8 means two.

Week one is your calibration week. Start lighter than you think on everything, because none of these movements have a number yet. Do the first set, see where it landed, then adjust.

  • First set felt like a 5? Go up on the next one.
  • Felt like a 9? Come down.
  • Landed on target? That's your weight for the week.

After that it's simple. Hit all your reps at or under the target RPE, go up a small amount next week. Missed reps, or a set felt like a 9 when the card says 7? Stay on the same weight and repeat it. That's not going backwards, that's how it's meant to work. Some weeks you'll sleep badly or come in off a hard match, and dropping the weight that day is the right call, not a failure.

cards.title: Food Is The Big One
cards.body:
You told me your eating is average and inconsistent, and you want to lose weight and look better. I'll be straight with you. The gym won't do that on its own. Three hours a week of training can't out-run seven days of food.

I'm not handing you a diet in week one. Start with two things and we'll build from there at your check-in.

  • Protein at every meal. A palm-sized portion of meat, fish, eggs or yoghurt, three or four times a day. This is what keeps your muscle while you lose fat.
  • Eat the same on tennis days and rest days. Most people eat well when they train and fall apart on the days off. That's where your inconsistency lives.

Weigh yourself twice a week, same time, first thing in the morning. Not every day. I'm looking at the direction over a month, not the number on a Tuesday.

cards.title: Film These Two Lifts
cards.body:
Two lifts in here can hurt you if the position is wrong, and I'm not standing next to you. The Goblet Squat and the Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift.

Film your heaviest set of both, from the side, once a week, and send them to me on WhatsApp. Thirty seconds of your time. It's the only way I can coach your technique from here.

On the Romanian deadlift the weight goes up only after I've seen the film and cleared your back position. If the videos stop coming, the weight stops moving. That one isn't negotiable. It's the lift with the most to lose.

cards.title: Tennis Days And Gym Days
cards.body:
You're playing three or four days and now training three more. That's six or seven days on your legs, and your tennis stays the priority. The gym is here to make you better on court, not to leave you flat for it.

Space the gym days out. Try not to put Day 1 and Day 2 next to each other if you can help it. Both of them work your lower back and it wants a day in between.

If a gym day lands on a tennis day, two rules:

  • Tennis first, gym after. Or leave four to six hours between them.
  • If you can't get that gap, do the first exercise of the session and go home. That's enough to keep the week alive.

cards.title: Sleep Is Your Cheapest Win
cards.body:
Seven to eight hours is fine. But you rated the quality a six out of ten, and that's the part worth fixing. Hours in bed aren't the same as hours asleep.

You're about to ask your body for more than it's used to. Going from one or two gym days to three, on top of your tennis, gets paid for somewhere, and sleep is where.

Pick one thing and do it for four weeks. Same bedtime every night, or phone out of the room, or no coffee after 4pm. One. Not all three. Tell me at the check-in whether that six moved.

cards.title: Why This Looks Simple
cards.body:
You might look at this and think it's too easy. Dumbbells, machines, a goblet squat, no barbell anywhere. That's on purpose.

You've got under a year in the gym and nobody has watched you move yet. Putting a loaded bar on your back in week one would be me guessing, and at ninety kilos I'm not guessing with your knees and your back.

The goblet squat has a ceiling built into it. When the heaviest dumbbell in that gym starts feeling easy, you've earned the barbell, and that's exactly what cycle two is. You're not being held back, you're being set up.

cards.title: Log Every Set
cards.body:
Log every set. Weight, reps, RPE. Ten seconds between sets, and it's the only thing I can see from here.

When I write your next cycle I'm reading these logs to decide which exercises stay, which get swapped, and where the rep and RPE targets go next. An empty log means I'm designing blind and you get a worse program for it.

Same with the readiness check before each session. Be honest on the bad days. A four out of ten tells me something useful. A fake eight tells me nothing.

cards.title: If You Only Get One Day
cards.body:
Busy week, bad sleep, tennis ran long. It happens. Do the first exercise of the session and call it done. Day 1 is the goblet squat, Day 2 is the Romanian deadlift, Day 3 is the reverse lunge.

On a day where you feel flat, take one point off every RPE on the card. A 7 becomes a 6. You still trained, you just didn't dig a hole.

You can also move the days around to fit your week. The order is what I'd pick, not a rule. A session you actually did beats the perfect one you skipped.
